name: Plant Respiration
author: @praisejamesx
tagline: Watch the plant, not just the number.
summary: A weekly plant-health workspace that pairs array response with light, water, leaf, and root context — and states what the array cannot see.
whatItIs: A structured log for one plant. It helps you notice a VOC or respiration change and correlate it with care, light, and visible symptoms.
whatItIsNot: Not ethylene detection, not a pest or pathogen diagnosis, not a substitute for inspecting roots and leaves, and not a cross-rig claim.
citations: Kesselmeier, J. & Staudt, M. (1999). Biogenic volatile organic compounds (VOC): an overview. Journal of Atmospheric Chemistry 33, 23–88.
Dicke, M. & Baldwin, I. T. (2010). The evolutionary context for herbivore-induced plant volatiles. Trends in Plant Science 15(3), 167–175.

widgets.title: Plant Respiration
widgets.subtitle: A weekly change log with roots, leaves, and light in the frame.
widgets.note: Example Vial · host-rendered · no executable code

widgets.headline: A change signal is not a diagnosis.
widgets.body: The array can notice that a plant’s volatile profile changed. It cannot tell you why. Check water, light, pests, roots, and recent moves.
always: Record light, watering, and leaf condition with every sample.
Inspect the roots and the undersides of leaves.
Quarantine new plants before placing them near others.
never: Never treat a sensor spike as a pest or disease identification.
Never assume the array can see ethylene; the current constants table has no ethylene response.
Never compare a plant’s reading to a different array or rig.

widgets.title: What this workspace is allowed to claim

items.label: Array can do
items.hint: Same plant, same array, same time of day, against a baseline.

items.label: Array cannot do
items.hint: No ethylene channel and no pathogen or pest identification.

items.label: Best signal
items.hint: A single reading is weak; a weekly trend plus symptoms is stronger.

widgets.title: The plant, as a checklist
widgets.caption: Click a point. The sensor is one clue; the plant body is the rest of the evidence.

hotspots.label: Leaf surface
hotspots.body: Look for spots, curling, yellowing, sticky honeydew, webbing, or a change in leaf gloss. Check the underside, not just the top.

hotspots.label: Stem
hotspots.body: Soft, black, or constricted stems are structural problems the array cannot name. Record them with the reading.

hotspots.label: Soil / pot
hotspots.body: Overwatering and poor drainage can look like a slow decline. Smell the soil, check moisture, and look for fungus gnats.

hotspots.label: Roots
hotspots.body: Root rot can be invisible above the pot. If the plant is declining without an obvious leaf cause, inspect the root ball.

hotspots.label: Sensor
hotspots.body: Same array, same distance, same time of day. Temperature and humidity are confounds; log them. The array sees a VOC mixture, not ethylene.

steps.label: Baseline
steps.body: Pick one plant and one location. Record light, watering, pot size, and leaf condition. Take a clean reference blank.

steps.label: Weekly
steps.body: Sample at the same time of day. Log the reading with water, light, leaf, and soil notes.

steps.label: Change
steps.body: A spike or drop is a prompt to inspect. Look for pests, root problems, drafts, or a recent move before changing care.

steps.label: Review
steps.body: Compare the trend, not one point. Re-baseline after a move, repot, or season change.

widgets.title: Smell index trend
widgets.note: The line is your log. A rise is a prompt to inspect, not a diagnosis. The current array has no ethylene channel.

widgets.title: What to do with a change

rules.then: Check water, heat, and root health. Isolate if pests are visible. Do not treat the number as the cause.

rules.when: Gradual rise plus sticky leaves or webbing
rules.then: Inspect for pests, especially under the leaves. Do not spray blindly.
Look at roots, drainage, and light. The array may be blind to the cause.
Re-baseline after the move. Do not compare readings across rooms or seasons.
Do not use smell as exposure measurement. Ventilate and seek appropriate guidance.

items.label: Roots / drainage checked
items.detail: If the plant is declining without a leaf cause.

items.label: Water and light logged
items.detail: Context is part of the measurement.

items.label: Same array and time of day
items.detail: Do not compare across rigs or rooms.

items.label: New plants quarantined
items.detail: Do not let a new plant share air with the baseline plant.

items.label: Re-baseline after a change
items.detail: A move or repot invalidates the old baseline.

widgets.title: Use this with your rig
widgets.body: Record a clean reference blank and a plant sample on the same array and at the same time of day. Compare with Check. If the arrays differ, the app will refuse the comparison.

docs.title: How to use this workspace
body: Pick one plant and one location. Fill the plant fields, then add a weekly reading with the smell index, leaf, soil, water, and any action.
A reading is a prompt to look, not a diagnosis. The plant body and the care context are the evidence.
Use Check to compare the plant sample to a clean reference on the same array. A difference is a change signal, not an identification.

docs.title: What the sensor is actually doing
body: Plants emit a mixture of biogenic volatile organic compounds. Wounding, ripening, and stress can change that mixture. A MOX array sees a combined response, not a single compound.
The current constants table has no ethylene response, so the app cannot make an ethylene claim. Do not use it to decide whether fruit will ripen or whether a plant is emitting ethylene.
Humidity, temperature, distance, and the room’s background air all affect the reading. Log them.

docs.title: What can go wrong
body: A change signal can be caused by watering, a draft, a new cleaning product, a person, or a different time of day. It is not specific to a pest or pathogen.
Pests and root problems can be present without a large VOC change. Inspect the plant.
A sensor that has drifted or been exposed to a strong VOC can report a change that is about the sensor, not the plant.

docs.title: How to validate a Vial on your rig
body: Record a clean reference and at least three plant samples on the same array, at the same time of day, with the same distance.
Use Check to compare the reference and the plant. Read the lower bound and the permutation p-value.
A sealed Vial is a closed-set claim on the array that produced the evidence. It is not a diagnosis and it is not transferable to another rig.

docs.title: References
body: Kesselmeier, J. & Staudt, M. (1999). Biogenic volatile organic compounds (VOC): an overview. Journal of Atmospheric Chemistry 33, 23–88.
Dicke, M. & Baldwin, I. T. (2010). The evolutionary context for herbivore-induced plant volatiles. Trends in Plant Science 15(3), 167–175.
These references describe plant VOC biology; they do not validate this Vial or turn a sensor response into a diagnosis.
